title: The Fluid and the Lake: Mesmer from Iznang to the Commission of the King and back to the Bodensee
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Iznang, birth on the Untersee shore
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinate corrected: the birth house at Hoeristrasse 10, Iznang, geocodes to 47.71495, 8.95704 and the village to 47.71542, 8.96012; an earlier working coordinate of 47.6958, 8.9779 fell in open water 2.5 km offshore.
stops.campa: In the fishing village of Iznang on the Untersee, the shallow western arm of Lake Constance, a son is born to Anton Mesmer, who keeps the woods for the prince-bishop of Constance. The child is christened Franz Anton. The Hoeristrasse house looks out on flat wet ground and a horizon of water, and the water outside that door is the same water he will die beside eighty years later, after Vienna, after Paris, after a royal commission of the King of France has examined the doctrine of his life and reported that it has no object.
suggested_refs: The birth house at Hoeristrasse 10, Iznang, commune of Moos am Bodensee

stops.name: Gruenenberg, the monastery school
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1742 to 1746; German Wikipedia states the Gruenenberg schooling flatly, citing Warndorf. Month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the Denkmal Kloster Gruenenberg marker at 47.69582, 8.95261, about 1 km from an earlier working figure.
stops.campa: The boy is sent along the Hoeri peninsula to the school at Gruenenberg for music and Latin. It is the ordinary ladder for a clever provincial child with no money behind him: the church teaches him and the church expects him back. He learns the language he will publish his propositions in thirty years later, and he learns music. Music stays with him through every room he ever practices in. The patients roped to his tub in Paris will convulse to a glass harmonica, and he will send for a player of one on the day he dies.
suggested_refs: The Kloster Gruenenberg memorial and the Burgstall above Gaienhofen

stops.name: Constance, the Jesuit college
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1746 to 1750; month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate corrected: German Wikipedia places the college at the present site of the Stadttheater Konstanz, Konzilstrasse 11, at 47.66384, 9.17742.
stops.campa: At the Jesuit college of Constance he studies within a few minutes' walk of the Muenster where the Council once tried Jan Hus and handed him over to the fire. The order that teaches him holds a cosmos strung with hidden correspondences, sympathies running between star and stone and living body. It is the order of Athanasius Kircher, who a hundred years before had argued in Rome that magnetism is the principle binding the world, one vast magnet of sympathies. Mesmer keeps the cosmology entire and changes only the name of the force.
suggested_refs: The site of the Konstanz Jesuit college, now the Stadttheater, Konzilstrasse 11
sources: kircher.journey.json (Rome, Magnes sive de Arte Magnetica, 1641)

stops.name: Dillingen an der Donau, logic and metaphysics
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1750 to 1754; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: At the Jesuit university of Dillingen on the Danube he reads logic, metaphysics and theology, the standard course for a boy meant for the priesthood. He is set on a road with one destination and no branches. Nothing in the record says why he leaves it. The record simply stops describing a future priest and begins describing a student of mathematics, physics and languages. The Society of Jesus trains him thoroughly and loses him, and he carries away everything it taught him except the vocation it taught him for.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit university buildings at Dillingen an der Donau

stops.name: Ingolstadt, theology set down
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1753; month and day unknown and defaulted. German Wikipedia's Dillingen and Ingolstadt spans overlap and are not reconciled in the source.
stops.campa: A short spell at the Jesuit college of Ingolstadt closes the theological training. He turns instead to mathematics, philosophy, physics and languages, the new sciences of a century that has decided the universe is a machine of forces acting where nothing touches. Newton has shown that bodies pull on one another across empty space. A young man raised on a cosmos of sympathies now learns that one of those sympathies can be measured and written down as an equation, and that the men who found it were not thought mad for looking.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit college of Ingolstadt, later absorbed into the university

segments.name: Vienna: the Planets and the Fluid

stops.name: Vienna, the Old University
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1759; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes to Vienna at twenty-five and enrolls in law, then leaves it for medicine under Gerard van Swieten and Anton de Haen, the Dutch reformers who have made the Vienna faculty the best clinical school in the Empire. Van Swieten is the Empress's own physician and the man the Habsburg lands send out to put down vampire panics and inspect miracle cures. Mesmer learns the bedside method from the two physicians in Europe most committed to stripping the marvellous out of medicine, and he learns it well.
suggested_refs: The Alte Universitaet on Dr.-Ignaz-Seipel-Platz, Vienna

stops.name: Vienna, the doctorate on planetary influx
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1766 after public disputation; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He defends De planetarum influxu in corpus humanum before the faculty: the planets act on the human body as the moon acts on the tides, through a fluid that fills all space, and the physician who learns its motions can read the sick and correct them. The thesis passes. It is orthodox enough in 1766 to pass without argument, and it contains, whole and already finished, the idea he will spend the next fifty years defending against every body of men ever appointed to examine it.
suggested_refs: De planetarum influxu in corpus humanum, Vienna, 1766

stops.name: Vienna, the palais on the Landstrasse
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage on 10 January 1768. Coordinate corrected to Palais Mesmer, Rasumofskygasse 29 (formerly Landstrasse 261), at 48.203163, 16.391392; earlier working figures of 48.1975, 16.385 and 48.197, 16.3891 were 700 to 900 m off. The Mozart tradition is hedged: German Wikipedia says the Bastien und Bastienne commission is repeatedly and wrongly given to Franz Anton and belonged to his cousin Joseph Conrad Mesmer, and Nissen found no proof.
stops.campa: He marries Maria Anna von Posch, a wealthy widow who owns Schloss Rothmuehle outside the city, and moves into the house on the Landstrasse that Vienna comes to call the Palais Mesmer. There is a garden, a laboratory, a private theater. The fashionable invalids of the imperial capital begin to arrive at the consulting room. A tradition puts the boy Mozart's Bastien und Bastienne in that garden in the year of the marriage, and the same tradition is claimed for his cousin Joseph Conrad, and Mozart's own biographer could find no proof of either.
suggested_refs: The Palais Mesmer site, Rasumofskygasse 29, Vienna Landstrasse

stops.name: Vienna, the magnets and Franziska Oesterlin
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1774; month and day unknown and defaulted. The two events, learning of Maximilian Hell's magnetic cures and the treatment of Franziska Oesterlin, are given under the same year by German and English Wikipedia respectively and are combined here.
stops.campa: Word reaches him of the Jesuit astronomer Maximilian Hell, who cures with steel magnets cut to the shape of the part they are laid on. Mesmer borrows the magnets and applies them, with an iron preparation, to Franziska Oesterlin, a young woman of his household whose convulsive attacks he has watched for years. She reports a current running down through her body. The attack breaks. He concludes at once that the steel is not the agent but the conductor, that the agent is in himself, and he gives the agent a name.
suggested_refs: Maximilian Hell's shaped steel magnets, Vienna, 1774

stops.name: Munich, judging the exorcist Gassner
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1775; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He is called to Munich to judge Johann Joseph Gassner, the priest whose exorcisms are curing the sick of Swabia in front of crowds. Mesmer does not call him a fraud. He says the cures are real and the explanation is wrong: Gassner is an unusually strong animal magnetizer who believes he is casting out devils. Then he produces the same convulsions in a subject himself, with no prayer and no crucifix. Gassner is silenced and sent to a country parish. Nine years later the commissioners of the King run the same argument against Mesmer in Paris.
suggested_refs: The Bavarian Academy of Sciences inquiry into Gassner's healings, Munich, 1775

stops.name: Vienna, the Sendschreiben on the magnetic cure
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1775; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He publishes the Sendschreiben an einen auswaertigen Arzt ueber die Magnetkur, an open letter to a foreign physician setting out the doctrine in public for the first time. A single fluid, universally diffused, admitting no vacuum, running between the stars and the nerves. Disease is obstruction of its flow. Cure is the crisis that clears the obstruction. He sends the letter out to the learned academies of Europe and waits to be examined by them, and this is the posture he will hold for the rest of his working life.
suggested_refs: Sendschreiben an einen auswaertigen Arzt ueber die Magnetkur, 1775

stops.name: Vienna, the sight of Maria Theresia Paradis
stops.date_confidence: attested for treatment from late 1776 to the middle of 1777 (English Wikipedia, 'Maria Theresia von Paradis'); the month here is an approximation of 'late 1776'. The pension motive attributed to her parents is in Wikipedia but contested in the literature: see Pattie, 'A Mesmer-Paradis Myth Dispelled', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis 22:1 (1979). English Wikipedia also states that the Empress was not her godmother.
stops.campa: Maria Theresia Paradis, a pianist blind since the age of three and pensioned by the court, is brought into the house on the Landstrasse. Under his hands her sight comes back in fragments, and the fragments are unbearable to her. She cannot play with her eyes open. Human faces disgust her. Her parents take her out of the house in the middle of the treatment, the blindness returns whole, and she goes on playing for another fifty years. Every surviving account of the quarrel comes from somebody with an interest in the outcome.
suggested_refs: The Paradis affair, Vienna, 1776 to 1777, and the sources assembled against it by Frank Pattie

stops.name: Vienna, the verdict and the departure
stops.date_confidence: attested: the imperial commission's finding of fraud is dated 1777 and the departure for Paris 20 January 1778 (German Wikipedia). Canonical Vienna pin inherited from freud.journey.json.
stops.campa: An imperial commission declares his methods fraudulent. The faculty that gave him his doctorate eleven years before will not defend him, and the drawing rooms that filled his consulting room stop sending. In January he leaves Vienna for Paris, forty-three years old, without his wife, carrying the doctrine to the one city where the Academy of Sciences is the highest court of scientific appeal in Europe. He goes there to be examined. The examination takes him six years to obtain and one afternoon to lose.
suggested_refs: The 1777 Vienna commission finding on the magnetic cure

segments.name: Paris: the Tub and the Subscription

stops.name: Creteil, first ground in France
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved. French Wikipedia has him halt at Creteil in May 1778 and only afterwards take the hotel Bourret on the Place Vendome; German Wikipedia dates the Place Vendome practice to February 1778, which would put the consulting room three months before the arrival. Both are recorded; neither is adopted over the other. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: His first ground in France is not Paris but Creteil, a village on the Marne at the edge of it, where he stops before entering the capital. He arrives with a doctrine and with the Paradis affair behind him, and his wife and his money are still in Austria. Within eighteen months the Faculty of Medicine, the Royal Society of Medicine and the Academy of Sciences will each have been asked to examine him, and the wives of ministers will be sitting in circles round a wooden tub in his rooms with iron rods held against their livers.
suggested_refs: Creteil on the Marne, the halt before Paris

stops.name: Place Vendome, the Hotel Bourret
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives February 1778 for the Place Vendome practice; French Wikipedia's sequence puts it after a May 1778 arrival at Creteil. The February date is used here and the conflict is left standing. Day defaulted. Coordinate within about 100 m of the Place Vendome centroid at 48.86746, 2.32943.
stops.campa: He opens at the Hotel Bourret on the Place Vendome, one of the most expensive addresses in Europe. He treats with his hands: long passes down the length of the body without touching it, a fixed stare, a thumb held at the pit of the stomach until the patient sweats or weeps or falls. The queen's circle takes him up. The Faculty of Medicine will not have him at any price. Neither position shifts for six years, and the Paris career is stretched between them until it tears.
stops.quote: The most sensible effects are produced on the approach of Mesmer, who is said to convey the fluid by certain motions of his hands or eyes, without touching the person.
stops.quote_source: Contemporary English doctor's eyewitness letter from Mesmer's Paris clinic, 1784, quoted in Lisa Morton, Calling the Spirits: A History of Seances (Reaktion Books, 2022)
suggested_refs: The Hotel Bourret on the Place Vendome, Mesmer's first Paris consulting rooms

stops.name: Geneva, the Memoire of twenty-seven propositions
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1779, printed at Geneva by P. Fr. Didot le jeune, eighty-five pages; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: The Memoire sur la decouverte du magnetisme animal is printed at Geneva, eighty-five pages, twenty-seven numbered propositions. It asks for nothing the physics of the age would call impossible: a subtle fluid, universally diffused, continuous, admitting no vacuum, carrying influence between the celestial bodies and the earth and the bodies of animated beings. Newton's aether had been argued in the same words. What the twenty-seven propositions do not contain is any experiment by which the fluid could be found or missed.
stops.quote: It is a fluid universally diffused; the vehicle of a mutual influence between the celestial bodies, the earth and the bodies of animated beings; it is so continued as to admit of no vacuum; its subtlety does not admit of illustration; it is capable of receiving, propagating and communicating all the impressions that are incident to motion.
stops.quote_source: Mesmer's account of his discovery, quoted in Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners, Charged by the King of France, with the Examination of the Animal Magnetism, as now practised at Paris (London: J. Johnson, 1785), p. 20
suggested_refs: Memoire sur la decouverte du magnetisme animal, Geneva, P. Fr. Didot le jeune, 1779

stops.name: Hotel Bullion, the great baquet
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia dates the group baquet treatment to 1780; French Wikipedia places the largest baquet at the hotel Bullion, at the corner of the rue Coq-Heron and the rue du Louvre, without a precise year. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Near Saint-Eustache, in the Hotel Bullion, he installs the largest of the tubs: oak, lidded, filled with bottled water and iron filings, bent iron rods rising through holes in the lid to whatever height the afflicted part requires. Patients sit in rings, joined at the thumbs by a cord. A glass harmonica plays in the next room. They cough, sweat, laugh, shriek, and fall into the crisis, and are carried out to a mattressed chamber to finish it. Twenty at a tub, and the tubs are full every day.
stops.quote: In the middle of the room is placed a vessel of about a foot and a half high which is called here a "baquet". It is so large that twenty people can easily sit round it; near the edge of the lid which covers it, there are holes pierced corresponding to the number of persons who are to surround it; into these holes are introduced iron rods, bent at right angles outwards, and of different heights, so as to answer to the part of the body to which they are to be applied.
stops.quote_source: Contemporary English doctor's eyewitness letter, 1784, quoted in Lisa Morton, Calling the Spirits: A History of Seances (Reaktion Books, 2022)
suggested_refs: The Hotel Bullion, corner of the rue Coq-Heron and the rue du Louvre, Paris

stops.name: Spa, the springs and the Precis historique
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia has him leave Paris in May 1781 and write the Precis at Spa; the book is dated London, 1781. Day defaulted. The page count is 229, not the 1,229 given in one working note.
stops.campa: He withdraws for a season to the mineral springs of Spa, the resort that has given its name to every such place since, and writes there the Precis historique des faits relatifs au magnetisme animal jusques en avril 1781, two hundred and twenty-nine pages carrying his own affair up to the spring of that year. He is at the height of his fame and he is writing out his grievances. Three learned bodies in Paris have declined to examine him on his terms. He has begun keeping the record himself, in his own hand.
suggested_refs: Precis historique des faits relatifs au magnetisme animal jusques en avril 1781, London, 1781

stops.name: Paris, the subscription of three hundred and forty thousand livres
stops.date_confidence: attested for the return to Paris and the Bergasse subscription in 1781 to 1782 (German Wikipedia). Month and day defaulted. The foundation of the Societe de l'Harmonie is a separate and later event and is not dated here. Canonical Paris pin inherited from gurdjieff.journey.json.
stops.campa: Nicolas Bergasse, a lawyer from Lyon, and the banker Guillaume Kornmann organize a subscription to refinance the practice: three hundred and forty thousand livres raised from private men, against which Mesmer undertakes to teach the doctrine to the subscribers. For six years he has asked the academies to examine him and they have not. He stops asking. What no faculty will certify he sells instead as a secret, and it is a lawyer and a banker, not a physician, who set the price of it.
stops.quote: It is a mistake, to imagine that this kind of proof is unanswerable; it cannot be demonstrated that either the physician or the medicine causes the recovery of the patient.
stops.quote_source: Mesmer, replying to an objection from a member of the Academy of Sciences, in Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785), p. 38
suggested_refs: The Bergasse and Kornmann subscription of 1781 to 1782

stops.name: Paris, the Societe de l'Harmonie universelle
stops.date_confidence: date contested and not resolved. French Wikipedia dates the Societe de l'harmonie universelle to 1784, founded with Bergasse and Kornmann; the usual scholarly date is 1783; one working note wrongly folded it into the 1781 subscription. 1784 is used here on the French Wikipedia authority. Month and day defaulted. German Wikipedia gives twenty affiliated societies.
stops.campa: The Societe de l'Harmonie universelle is constituted with Bergasse and Kornmann to hold the teaching and spread it: initiates sworn to secrecy, a subscription paid at the door, daughter societies in twenty towns of France. The doctrine now has a membership, a treasury and a rite, and it has all three before it has a proof. In the rooms of the society the tub does what the tub has always done, and in the same season the King of France is choosing the men who will be sent to sit beside it and watch.
stops.quote: Some of them are calm, tranquil and unconscious to any sensation; others cough, spit, are affected with a slight degree of pain, a partial or an universal burning, and perspirations; a third class are agitated and tormented with convulsions.
stops.quote_source: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785), p. 26, describing patients around the baquet
suggested_refs: The Societe de l'Harmonie universelle and its twenty provincial affiliates

stops.name: Passy, the blindfolded boy in Franklin's garden
stops.date_confidence: attested: the report itself states that the king named four physicians of the Faculty of Paris on the twelfth of March 1784, with the Academy of Sciences members joined to them; the trials were conducted partly at Franklin's residence at Passy.
stops.campa: Louis XVI names the commission in March: four physicians of the Faculty, and from the Academy of Sciences Benjamin Franklin, Antoine Lavoisier, Jean Sylvain Bailly, Jean d'Arcet, Gabriel de Bory and Joseph-Ignace Guillotin. Franklin is seventy-eight and too gouty to be carried into the city, so the commission comes out to him at Passy. In his garden they magnetize one tree of four and walk a blindfolded boy down the row. He falls into the crisis at the third tree. The third tree is not the one.
stops.quote: The boy fell into a crisis under a tree which was not magnetised; the crisis was therefore the effect of no physical or exterior cause, but is to be ascribed solely to the influence of imagination.
stops.quote_source: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785), p. 69
suggested_refs: Franklin's house and garden at Passy, site of the tree experiment
sources: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (1785), Project Gutenberg ebook 78413

stops.name: Paris, the clinic of Charles Deslon
stops.date_confidence: attested that both commissions examined Deslon's practice and not Mesmer's: 'The commission did not examine Mesmer specifically, but instead observed the practice of d'Eslon' (English Wikipedia). Month and day are inferred from the commission's working period and defaulted; the coordinate is a round-number placeholder for a Paris address not established in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The commission never examines Mesmer. He will not accept their terms, so they test the practice of Charles Deslon, physician to the Comte d'Artois, his first Paris disciple and now his rival, who has carried the doctrine into the open without permission. Deslon gives them everything: the rod, the tub, the passes, his patients, his declarations in writing. Every published result about animal magnetism is therefore a result about Deslon's rooms. When the verdict comes he accepts it, and says imagination so directed would be valuable in a physician's hands.
stops.quote: That this rod is a conductor of the magnetism, has the power of concentring it at its point, and of rendering its emanations more considerable.
stops.quote_source: Charles Deslon, first of his declarations to the commissioners, in Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785), p. 24
suggested_refs: Charles Deslon's declarations to the royal commissioners, 1784
sources: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (1785)

stops.name: The Louvre, the report to the King
stops.date_confidence: attested: the report is dated 'Paris, the 11th day of August, 1784' and was presented to the King. One working note had it presented to the Academy of Sciences on that date and gave the twelfth; both are wrong. The coordinate is the Academie Royale des Sciences seat at the Louvre and stands for the institutional setting, not for a delivery to the Academy.
stops.campa: The report goes to the King on the eleventh of August. Bailly writes it. The signatures under it are Franklin, Majault, Le Roy, Sallin, Bailly, d'Arcet, de Bory, Guillotin, Lavoisier. The finding is not that the patients are lying: the commissioners have sat beside the tub and set down the convulsions in clinical detail. The finding is that nothing can be detected passing to any body that does not already know it is being treated. The blindfold is the instrument, and medicine will later call this design a blinded trial and date its own use of it from here.
stops.quote: The commissioners... concluded with an unanimous voice respecting the existence and the utility of the magnetism, that the existence of the fluid is absolutely destitute of proof, that the fluid having no existence can consequently have no use.
stops.quote_source: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785), p. 106; the sentence continues, ascribing the violent symptoms to compression, to the imagination called into action, and to mechanical imitation
suggested_refs: The Franklin Commission report of 11 August 1784, London translation of 1785
sources: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (1785), Project Gutenberg ebook 78413

stops.name: Paris, the second report and the one dissent
stops.date_confidence: attested for 16 August 1784, five days after the Franklin report. The coordinate for the Societe Royale de Medecine is approximate and was not independently verified. This commission was not unanimous: Antoine Laurent de Jussieu dissented and issued a separate report, which qualifies the 'unanimous scientific weight' sometimes claimed for the year's verdict as a whole.
stops.campa: Five days later the commission of the Royal Society of Medicine reports separately and arrives in the same place by the same road: the sensations are real, the fluid is not, and imagination alone will produce heat, pain and crisis in any part of a body that expects them. One commissioner refuses to sign. Antoine Laurent de Jussieu, the botanist, files a dissenting report of his own arguing that something physical does pass between operator and patient. It is filed, printed, and left where it lies.
stops.quote: They were therefore convinced that the imagination alone is capable of producing various sensations, and causing the patient to experience both pain and heat, and even a very considerable degree of heat, in all parts of the body.
stops.quote_source: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785), pp. 64-65, on the blindfold experiment
suggested_refs: The Societe Royale de Medecine report of 16 August 1784 and the separate report of A. L. de Jussieu

stops.name: Buzancy, the sleep of Victor Race
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1784 at Buzancy (English Wikipedia, 'Animal magnetism'); month and day unknown and defaulted. The coordinate is the commune of Buzancy in the Aisne and is supplied here from general geography, not from any source in the verified pool.
stops.campa: At Buzancy a marquis who took the doctrine from the Paris society magnetizes a young man named Victor Race. He does not convulse. He falls into a lucid sleep, speaks, answers questions, diagnoses his own illness, and remembers nothing at all on waking. Puysegur has found, in the same year the commissioners are walking blindfolded boys past trees, the one thing nobody had been appointed to look for. Somnambulism, hypnotism, suggestion and the talking cure all descend from this man asleep in a field, and not from the tub.
stops.quote: These convulsions are characterised by precipitate and involuntary motions of all the limbs or of the whole body, by a contraction of the throat, by sudden affections of the hypochonders and the epigastrium, by a distraction and wildness in the eyes, by shrieks, tears, hiccuppings, and immoderate laughter.
stops.quote_source: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785), p. 26, describing the crisis as practised at the baquet
suggested_refs: The Marquis de Puysegur's account of Victor Race at Buzancy, 1784

stops.name: Paris, the last departure
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia dates the final departure from Paris to 1785; German Wikipedia describes the departure from France more loosely as 1784 to 1788, with travel through England and the German lands. Month and day defaulted. Canonical Paris pin inherited.
stops.campa: He leaves Paris. The commission has forbidden nothing and stopped nobody, and there are more magnetizers in France after the verdict than before it, but the thing he came for has been given to him and has gone against him. He does not accept it and he does not stay to fight it. He is fifty years old and rich, by his own later reckoning a millionaire in French paper, and he will spend the next thirty years moving between countries that have all read the report and none of which can undo it.
stops.quote: Our conclusion is, that the imagination singly produces all the effects attributed to the magnetism, and that, where the imagination ceases to be called forth, it has no longer the smallest efficacy.
stops.quote_source: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785), concluding the experiment on mademoiselle B----; the original opens 'The inevitable conclusion is'
suggested_refs: The dispersal of Mesmer's Paris practice after August 1784

stops.name: London, the years under another name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. French Wikipedia reports the English residence under an assumed identity; no address, no patient and no year within the span are established. German Wikipedia says only that he travelled through England and the German lands between 1784 and 1788. Dated here to the start of that span with month and day defaulted. Canonical London pin, as used in bulwer_lytton.journey.json.
stops.campa: He is said to spend these years in England, in London, under a name that is not his own, keeping clear of French creditors and French notoriety together. No address is known. No patient is named. Biographers who can follow him street by street through Vienna and Paris give the English years a paragraph and move on. The doctrine crosses the Channel without him in the same decade, and will be practised in London parlours and provincial lecture halls for sixty years under a word coined from his surname.
suggested_refs: The gap in the record: Mesmer's English residence, c. 1785 to 1789

stops.name: Karlsruhe, the Margrave's recognition
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1788; day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: The Margrave Karl Friedrich of Baden, an enlightened prince with a taste for natural philosophy, extends recognition to the teaching on magnetism, and Mesmer comes to Karlsruhe. This is the shape of the wandering years: a German court, a hearing, a season of respect, no institution and no chair. The Paris report travels faster than he does and is read at every court before he reaches it. He is a famous man calling on the courts that will still receive him, and not one of them offers him a post.
suggested_refs: The court of Margrave Karl Friedrich of Baden at Karlsruhe

stops.name: Vienna, arrested as a Jacobin
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival 14 September 1793, detention 17 November, release 9 December, exile under surveillance to the region of his birth. French Wikipedia also reports a Vienna return in 1790, which German Wikipedia does not have at all; the wife's death is placed in 1790 by German Wikipedia, with the couple then living apart. Canonical Vienna pin inherited.
stops.campa: He comes back to Vienna in September, sixteen years after the city closed to him and three years after his wife died there while they were living apart. Austria is at war with the French Republic, and a man who has spent twenty years in Paris is a suspect by arithmetic. On the seventeenth of November he is arrested for Jacobin sympathies, held three weeks, released on the ninth of December and expelled under police surveillance to the district he was born in. The Empire sends him back to the lake by order.
suggested_refs: The Vienna police file of November 1793 on Mesmer's detention

stops.name: Wagenhausen, a Swiss residence bought
stops.date_confidence: attested: Thurgau residency rights acquired 1794, residence at Wagenhausen 1794 to 1798. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Wagenhausen TG at 47.65963, 8.84849, about 3 km from an earlier working figure. The often repeated detail that he kept bees here is in no source consulted and is omitted.
stops.campa: He buys residency rights in the canton of Thurgau and settles at Wagenhausen on the Rhine below Lake Constance, a village of a few hundred souls with a former priory and a bridge. He treats whoever comes to the door. He is a Swiss now, by purchase, in a confederation that has no academy to refuse him and no police to expel him. In France the assignat is destroying the fortune he made there, and the societies that paid three hundred and forty thousand livres for his secret have gone down with the monarchy.
suggested_refs: Wagenhausen on the Rhine, canton of Thurgau

stops.name: Paris, creditor of the state
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1798: German Wikipedia, citing Kerner, has him obtain an annual pension of 3,000 francs as creancier d'etat, payable also into Germany. One working note claimed he sought a pension unsuccessfully; that is the opposite of the source. Month and day defaulted. Canonical Paris pin inherited.
stops.campa: He returns to France and petitions the Republic as a creancier d'etat, a creditor of the state, for the value of holdings the Revolution has destroyed. He is granted three thousand francs a year, payable to him abroad. It is the only official act any French government ever performs in his favour, and it settles a debt rather than reverses a verdict. The report of 1784 stands exactly where the commissioners left it. The doctrine stays condemned; the man who wrote it is put back on the books and paid.
suggested_refs: The French state pension of 3,000 francs granted to Mesmer in 1798
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Franz Anton Mesmer' (citing Justinus Kerner)

stops.name: Versailles, writing into an emptied country
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move to Versailles in February 1801; day defaulted. The Memoire sur ses decouvertes is dated 1799 and the Briefe ueber den Ursprung der Blattern 1800, both within the 1798 to 1801 French period.
stops.campa: He takes rooms at Versailles, in the emptied town beside the emptied palace, having published in these French years the Memoire sur ses decouvertes and the Briefe ueber den Ursprung der Blattern, letters on the origin of smallpox. He is sixty-six and writing for a readership that no longer exists in the country he is writing in. The men who signed the report against him are dead or scattered by the Revolution, and the report has outlived all of them and is still the standing verdict wherever the question is raised.
suggested_refs: Memoire sur ses decouvertes (1799) and Briefe ueber den Ursprung der Blattern (1800)

stops.name: Riedetsweiler, the hamlet above Meersburg
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives the return as the winter of 1802 to 1803; the closing year of the stay is inferred from the 1808 move to Frauenfeld and is a reconstruction. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the Riedetsweiler hamlet node at 47.70350, 9.28956, about 4 km from an earlier working figure.
stops.campa: In the winter he crosses back over the lake to Riedetsweiler, a farming hamlet in the hills north of Meersburg, close enough to see the water from the fields. He is twenty-five miles from Iznang. Everything that happened to him, the doctorate, the palais, the tub, the King's commission, the arrest, happened in the sixty-eight years between one shore of this lake and this hillside above the other. He treats farmers here. No record survives of what, if anything, he charges them for it.
suggested_refs: Riedetsweiler, north of Meersburg, in the Baden hill country above the Bodensee

stops.name: Frauenfeld, the papers handed to Wolfart
stops.date_confidence: attested: residence at Frauenfeld 1808 to 1812, practising largely without charge, and the reception of Karl Christian Wolfart in September 1808. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: He takes a house on the Zuercherstrasse in Frauenfeld, capital of the canton, and practises largely without charge. In September the Berlin physician Karl Christian Wolfart arrives, sent to find out whether the man is alive and what he actually taught. Mesmer gives him the papers of forty years. Wolfart will publish them in 1814 as Mesmerismus oder System der Wechselwirkungen, lose most of the manuscripts afterwards, and print his teacher's given name on the title page as Friedrich.
suggested_refs: Mesmerismus oder System der Wechselwirkungen, ed. K. C. Wolfart, Berlin, 1814

stops.name: Constance, the Hardthaus on the Hussenstrasse
stops.date_confidence: contradiction resolved against one source and recorded. The body text of German Wikipedia gives December 1808 for this move; that is contradicted by its own preceding section, by its photograph caption reading 'Wohnung von Franz Anton Mesmer von 1812 bis 1814', and by de.wikipedia 'Hussenstrasse', which states that Mesmer lived in the Hardthaus at Hussenstrasse 17 from 1812 to 1814. December 1812 is used; day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the building 'Zum Hardthaus' at 47.65999, 9.17274.
stops.campa: He moves into the Hardthaus at Hussenstrasse 17 in Constance, on the street named for Jan Hus, who lodged in it before the Council of Constance handed him to the fire. Sixty-six years earlier Mesmer studied at the Jesuit college a few hundred paces from this door. He is seventy-eight years old. The city that educated him takes him back as a private gentleman with a Swiss residence permit and a French pension, and there is nobody in it who needs to be told what animal magnetism is.
suggested_refs: The house 'Zum Hardthaus', Hussenstrasse 17, Konstanz

stops.name: Constance, the testament in his own hand
stops.date_confidence: attested for 11 April 1814. The passage of the diploma and seal ring to Justinus Kerner is a secondary characterization in German Wikipedia's estate summary and is a reconstruction as to the route by which they reached him.
stops.campa: He writes out his will in his own hand: a simple burial, no ceremony, and an autopsy. The man whose fluid the Academy of Sciences could not detect with any instrument in Paris asks to be opened and looked at in Constance. His doctoral diploma and his seal ring pass afterwards to the physician-poet Justinus Kerner at Weinsberg, who keeps them with the papers of his own somnambulist patients, so that the diploma the Vienna faculty granted in 1766 ends up in a cabinet of magnetic sleepwalkers.
suggested_refs: Mesmer's holograph testament, Constance, 11 April 1814

stops.name: Riedetsweiler, the last summer
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summer of 1814 at Sebastian Futterer's farmstead, formerly the inn 'zu den Drei Luemmeln'; month and day approximate within that summer and defaulted. Coordinate as corrected for Riedetsweiler.
stops.campa: He spends the summer back at Riedetsweiler, in a converted barn on the farmstead of Sebastian Futterer, formerly the inn called zu den Drei Luemmeln. He is eighty. The building that replaces it in 1912 will carry his coat of arms cut into the wall with the date of this summer under it, set where it cannot be seen from the road. It is the last address in his life that he chooses rather than accepts, and he holds it for one season before his relatives find him a room.
suggested_refs: The Futterer farmstead at Riedetsweiler and the concealed Mesmer arms dated 1814 at Baitenhauser Strasse 5

stops.name: Meersburg, the pensioner's room in the Heilig-Geist-Spital
stops.date_confidence: attested for the autumn of 1814; month approximate and day defaulted. Corrected in one detail: the room is the Pfruendnerstube on the first floor, one storey up, not a ground-floor room. The coordinate follows the corrected death-house figure 47.6938, 9.2731; a nearby working figure of 47.6942, 9.2664 is about 510 m west, and the street address given elsewhere is Vorburggasse 11.
stops.campa: In the autumn his nephew Cajetan Strommayer, administrator of the Heilig-Geist-Spital at Meersburg, arranges the pensioner's room on the first floor for him. He moves in with his housekeeper, his servant and his maid. Out of the window there is the lake. He is an almsman of a hospital, quartered by a relative, in a small town on the northern shore, at the end of a life in which he was received by the Empress's physician, the Bavarian academy, the queen's circle in Paris, and eventually by no institution at all.
suggested_refs: The Heilig-Geist-Spital at Meersburg, now the Vineum Bodensee

stops.name: Meersburg, death waiting for the glass harmonica
stops.date_confidence: attested: illness from 26 February 1815, death by stroke 5 March 1815, aged 80. The deathbed detail is a contemporary account reported in German Wikipedia and carries the weight of a contemporary account, no more.
stops.campa: He falls ill at the end of February and dies on the fifth of March, of a stroke, eighty years old. He has asked for music. A player of the glass harmonica, the instrument that sounded over the tubs in the Hotel Bullion, has been sent for and does not arrive in time. The contemporary account says that he died composedly, smiling, still waiting for it. The autopsy he asked for in his will is performed, and nothing is found inside him that is not inside anybody else.
suggested_refs: The contemporary account of Mesmer's death at Meersburg, 5 March 1815

stops.name: Meersburg cemetery, the monument of 1830
stops.date_confidence: attested for erection in 1830 and renovation in 1902; month and day unknown and defaulted. The plot is precisely located by German Wikipedia beside the Hochkreuz, about 10 m from the western cemetery wall, at 47.696006, 9.278171; an earlier working coordinate of 47.6889, 9.2694 fell outside the cemetery.
stops.campa: Fifteen years after the burial the Berlin Gesellschaft der Naturforscher pays for a monument, cut by the sculptor Sporer of Constance and set beside the high cross, ten metres from the western wall of the Meersburg cemetery: a triangular block of white marble on three graduated sandstone steps. East face, the radiating eye of providence above his name. Northwest, the solar system in concentric circles beside 23 May 1734. Southwest, a burning torch crossed with a palm beside 5 March 1815. On the top surface, a compass and a sundial.
suggested_refs: Mesmer's grave monument, Friedhof Meersburg, erected 1830, renovated 1902

stops.name: London, the practice keeps the name and drops the physics
stops.date_confidence: attested for Braid's coinage of 'hypnotism' in 1843 and his 1851 repudiation of 'Transcendental Mesmerism'; month and day unknown and defaulted. The coordinate is the canonical London pin standing for Britain as a whole; Braid himself practised in Manchester, and no location is given for these events in the verified pool.
stops.campa: In Britain the practitioners keep the practice and drop the physics. They call it mesmerism, after him, precisely so as to stop calling it magnetism. James Braid coins hypnotism in 1843 and by 1851 is repudiating what he names Transcendental Mesmerism outright, explaining the whole business as a state of the nervous system induced by fixed attention. Edward Bulwer-Lytton fills his novels with mesmerists in these same decades, and writes to John Forster that the vril of his last book means electricity and not mesmerism.
suggested_refs: James Braid, Neurypnology (1843) and his 1851 repudiation of Transcendental Mesmerism

stops.name: Paris, the Salpetriere and the clinical descendants
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the lineage. The Salpetriere pin is inherited byte for byte from delsarte.journey.json, where Delsarte visits the asylum around 1835 to study the gestures of the mad; Freud's Vienna practice advertising electrotherapy and hypnotic suggestion follows his return from Charcot and is attested in freud.journey.json. Neither journey names Mesmer, and the genealogical link from animal magnetism through Charcot to Freud is a historian's inference, not a documented citation. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: At the Salpetriere, the vast asylum where Francois Delsarte came in the eighteen-thirties to study the gestures of the mad, Jean-Martin Charcot turns hypnosis into a clinical instrument and hysteria into a Tuesday lecture with an audience. Sigmund Freud comes from Vienna to watch him and goes home burning with the example, opening a practice that advertises electrotherapy and hypnotic suggestion. The fluid is gone from the account. The operator, the susceptible patient, the crisis and the room arranged around them are all still standing.
suggested_refs: Charcot's Tuesday lectures at the Salpetriere and the Nancy school that opposed them

stops.name: Paris, the trick film and the long ridicule
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1905 Melies satire and for several hundred books on animal magnetism and its offshoots published between 1766 and 1925; month and day unknown and defaulted. The Schelling and Gurdjieff connections are reconstructions of intellectual descent: neither journey cites Mesmer by name. Canonical Paris pin inherited.
stops.campa: Across the nineteenth century Mesmer becomes a figure of ridicule, caricatured on the stage, and in 1905 Georges Melies puts him in a satirical short film. Between 1766 and 1925 several hundred books are published on animal magnetism and its offshoots. Schelling had taken the unified force into philosophy in 1798, with magnetism, electricity, chemistry and life as grades of one power, while Mesmer was alive in a Swiss village. Gurdjieff reads the hypnotism literature as a young man and sets up in Tashkent as professor of supernatural sciences.
suggested_refs: Georges Melies, satirical short on Mesmer, 1905

stops.name: Iznang, the bust on the shore
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2013 Zilly bust at Iznang; month and day unknown and defaulted. Peter Lenk's 'Magische Saeule' on the Meersburg harbour mole is attested without a year in the sources consulted. Coordinate corrected: Iznang is at 47.71542, 8.96012 with its shorefront just south, so about 47.7135, 8.9585; an earlier working figure of 47.7139, 8.9928 fell 2.4 km east toward Gundholzen.
stops.campa: A bronze bust by Friedhelm Zilly is set up in the shore installation by the harbour at Iznang, part of the commune of Moos, a few hundred metres from the house on the Hoeristrasse. Across the water at Meersburg, on the harbour mole, Peter Lenk's Magische Saeule shows him gripping a horseshoe magnet larger than his own body, which is the instrument he borrowed from a Jesuit astronomer and discarded inside a year. The two ends of the life are marked in bronze and stone and face each other across the lake.
suggested_refs: Friedhelm Zilly's 2013 bust at Iznang and Peter Lenk's 'Magische Saeule' at Meersburg

stops.name: Vienna, a plaque on a building that is not the house
stops.date_confidence: attested for 2019 at Rasumofskygasse 29, on the building erected in 1920 over the site of the former Palais Mesmer; month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to 48.203163, 16.391392; an earlier working figure of 48.1919, 16.3838 was 1.4 km off.
stops.campa: A plaque goes up at Rasumofskygasse 29 in the Landstrasse district, on a block raised in 1920 over the site of the palais where he married, kept a laboratory and a theater, magnetized Franziska Oesterlin, and gave Maria Theresia Paradis back her sight for long enough to lose it again. The palais itself is gone. Vienna commemorates an address rather than a house, two hundred and forty-two years after the imperial commission that met in this city called the practice conducted at it a fraud.
suggested_refs: The 2019 commemorative plaque at Rasumofskygasse 29, Vienna
